title: Build a Personal Finance Control Sheet
meta_description: Build a secure personal finance control sheet for accounts, cash flow, net worth, goals, debt, investments, records and monthly decisions.

sections.heading: Build a Control Sheet, Not a Data Museum
paragraphs: The opening photograph shows a laptop, tablet, calculator and handwritten analysis sharing one desk. That is the right visual for a personal finance control sheet: several sources brought into one decision surface. The aim is not to collect every transaction forever. It is to show what changed, what requires action and which evidence supports the number.

A useful workbook answers five questions quickly: How much cash is available? What is due before the next income? Is net worth moving for the intended reason? Which goal is off course? What decision needs an owner and date? If the file cannot answer these, more tabs will only create a larger archive.

Choose one control file and one evidence location. The control file contains summaries, calculations and action status. Evidence contains statements, invoices, contracts and tax records under appropriate retention rules. Do not embed passwords, full card numbers or identity documents in the workbook merely because everything feels convenient in one place.

Design for a thirty-minute monthly close and a deeper quarterly review. A system that requires daily categorisation or expert formulas will usually decay. Start with the minimum fields needed for reconciliation, then add detail only when it changes a recurring decision. Maintenance time is part of the tool’s cost.

Separate observed values from plans. Bank balance, debt balance and paid income are observed. Next month’s spending, expected bonus and investment return are assumptions. Use distinct columns or styling so a hopeful forecast cannot quietly become reported fact. Every dashboard figure should trace to a source, formula or clearly marked estimate.

Give the workbook a version, owner, last-updated date and review status. Those four fields prevent an old export from masquerading as the current plan. For couples or households, define who closes each section and who reviews it. Shared access should create continuity, not simultaneous edits with no accountability.

sections.heading: Define the Data Dictionary Before Entering Numbers
paragraphs: Create a short dictionary listing every field, unit, sign convention and source. Decide whether expenses are positive amounts in an expense table or negative amounts in a cash ledger. Decide whether dates use transaction, posting or statement date. Consistency is more valuable than a clever formula nobody can explain six months later.

Use stable identifiers for accounts and goals rather than relying on names alone. A bank can rebrand, and two cards can share the same nickname. An internal code such as CASH-01 or DEBT-02 lets formulas survive display-name changes without exposing full account numbers.

Define household boundaries. State which individual, joint, business, trust or dependent accounts are included. Personal net worth becomes misleading when a business balance is counted as household cash while its liabilities remain elsewhere. Record ownership and currency explicitly, then consolidate only under a documented rule.

Choose a base currency and preserve original currency for foreign balances. Record the conversion rate and date rather than overwriting the source value. Currency movement should be distinguishable from contributions, spending or investment return. Otherwise a change in exchange rate can look like saving.

Create an allowed category list with examples and exclusions. Housing might include rent and council tax but exclude furniture; transport might include fares and fuel but exclude a vehicle purchase. Keep the list short enough to apply consistently. New categories need a decision purpose, not merely a unique merchant.

Add validation rules where the tool permits them: approved account codes, real dates, numeric amounts and controlled status values. Validation catches typing errors before charts amplify them. It does not prove the underlying transaction is correct, so reconciliation with statements remains necessary.

sections.heading: Construct the Account Register First
paragraphs: The account register is the workbook’s map. List institution, account code, type, owner, currency, access class, interest or borrowing rate, payment date, statement date, insurance or protection status, and whether the account is active. Avoid storing login details or security answers.

Classify accounts by purpose: operating cash, emergency cash, sinking fund, investment, retirement, credit, loan or property. Purpose prevents the same cash being promised to several goals. A savings account can hold multiple purposes only if sub-balances reconcile to the provider total.

Record current balance and verified date. A balance without a date is not current; a date without a source is not verified. Link to a secure evidence folder or note the statement name rather than embedding sensitive files in a broadly shared sheet.

Track availability separately from value. A pension, term deposit and current account may all be assets, but they solve different liquidity needs. Add columns for immediate, restricted and long-term access. The dashboard can then show accessible cash without pretending retirement wealth is an emergency fund.

Mark dormant, closed and replaced accounts instead of deleting history. Closing an account should stop new imports and calculations while preserving prior periods. Record closure confirmation and any remaining statement retention. Deletion can break reconciliations and hide where a transfer originated.

Review the register quarterly for duplicated accounts, old rates, changed fees and missing beneficiaries or authorised users where relevant. Use provider documents and official channels. The register is an operational inventory, not evidence that a product remains suitable.

sections.heading: Turn Transactions Into a Reconciled Cash Ledger
paragraphs: Import or enter transactions from statements, not memory. Use date, account code, description, amount, category, transfer flag, review flag and evidence reference. Preserve the raw description in one column and place any cleaned merchant label in another so the original record remains available for audit.

Detect transfers before measuring spending. A card payment is not a second expense when the card purchases are already categorised; movement from current account to savings is not consumption. Match transfers by amount, date and accounts, allowing for settlement delays. Unmatched transfers stay flagged until explained.

Reconcile opening balance plus net transactions to closing balance for every account and period. A zero difference is the minimum condition for trust. It does not prove categories are correct, but a nonzero difference proves something is missing, duplicated or signed incorrectly.

The midpoint photograph shows a person surrounded by receipts, cash, a calculator and a laptop. It makes source records visible. Attach evidence only where it matters—tax, reimbursement, warranty, disputed charge or major purchase—rather than photographing every routine transaction without a retention purpose.

Use a review queue for uncategorised, unusual or duplicate-looking entries. Give each item an owner, question and deadline. Do not bury unresolved amounts in “miscellaneous.” A temporary suspense category can hold them, but the month cannot close while the suspense balance is material.

Lock or archive a reconciled period according to the tool’s capabilities. Corrections should create a dated adjustment note, not silently rewrite history. This allows comparisons to explain what was known at the time and prevents a formula change from altering several years without notice.

sections.heading: Build Cash Flow Around Timing, Not Averages
paragraphs: Create a monthly cash-flow view using actual take-home income and paid expenses. Show recurring and irregular items separately. Annual insurance, travel, gifts, school costs or professional fees become monthly sinking-fund contributions rather than surprises hidden by an average.

Add a due-date calendar for income, bills, debt minimums and transfers. A profitable month can still overdraw when payments arrive before income. Display the lowest projected operating balance, not only month-end cash. Timing is an operating risk that totals alone conceal.

Use three scenarios: committed, expected and optional. Committed includes contractual bills and minimums; expected adds normal variable essentials; optional includes flexible spending and extra goal transfers. This sequence shows what can be paused during disruption without calling essentials discretionary.

Compare plan with actual by category and total, but investigate only meaningful variance. A rigid limit on every small line creates review fatigue. Set thresholds by amount or percentage and focus on recurring drift, missing income, new commitments and categories that threaten cash or goals.

Do not count a credit-card limit, expected bonus or tax refund as available cash. Forecast income only when timing and amount are sufficiently reliable, and label it pending until cleared. The dashboard should become more conservative when uncertainty rises, not fill the gap with optimistic inputs.

Link every cash-flow action to the next pay cycle: transfer, cancel, negotiate, reserve or accept. A variance chart without a decision is decoration. Record who will act, by when, and how completion will be verified on the next statement.

sections.heading: Make Net Worth Explain the Movement
paragraphs: Create a dated balance snapshot for cash, investments, retirement accounts, property or business interests where included, and every liability. Use conservative, documented valuation methods. Personal possessions generally belong outside financial net worth unless a realistic resale value serves a defined planning purpose.

Calculate opening net worth plus contributions, debt principal, withdrawals and market or valuation movement to closing net worth. The bridge explains whether progress came from behaviour, price changes or new information. A higher balance caused by markets is different from a higher balance caused by saving.

Show total and accessible net worth side by side. Total includes restricted retirement assets; accessible excludes money that cannot reasonably meet a near-term obligation. A household can be progressing long term while remaining cash fragile. Both truths need a place on the control sheet.

Separate debt principal from interest and fees. Principal reduction increases net worth; interest and fees are expenses. A single payment figure cannot explain either. Record current settlement balance and rate where available, then reconcile it to lender statements.

Use valuation ranges for illiquid assets rather than a flattering single estimate. Record the method, evidence date, sale costs and any debt secured against the asset. Do not update property or private business values monthly unless reliable evidence supports that frequency.

Add a note for structural changes such as inheritance, account discovery, marriage, separation or a revised valuation method. Without a note, the chart can misrepresent a change in scope as investment performance or disciplined saving.

sections.heading: Give Every Goal a Funding Contract
paragraphs: Create a goal register with purpose, owner, target range, target date, current designated balance, required periodic contribution, priority and next review. A goal must identify the account or sub-balance holding its money. Otherwise the same savings balance can appear to fund emergency cash, travel and a deposit simultaneously.

Separate minimum viable, target and stretch outcomes. A home repair may have a required minimum; travel can scale; retirement is a long-horizon contribution process rather than one precise finish line. Ranges keep the sheet useful when prices or life plans change.

Calculate required contribution from the remaining gap and periods without assuming investment return for short-term goals. For long-term goals, show contributions separately from an optional return assumption and disclose that the assumption is uncertain. Never let a forecasted return substitute for an affordable contribution decision.

Create funding precedence for conflicts. Essential reserves and contractual obligations usually constrain optional goals, but the household should write its own sequence. When a new goal appears, identify which contribution, date or spending choice changes rather than letting total planned transfers exceed income.

Record goal withdrawals and purpose. A planned withdrawal is success, not negative saving, if it purchases the intended outcome. The net-worth bridge should label it so the dashboard does not punish the household for using money correctly.

Close completed or abandoned goals with a note directing any residual balance. Retaining dozens of inactive goals clutters alerts and hides priorities. History can remain archived without appearing in the current operating view.

sections.heading: Run Debt From a Payoff Queue
paragraphs: Build a debt register with lender, account code, balance, rate, minimum, due date, promotional expiry, security, term and any relevant early-settlement rule. Verify figures from current statements. The original borrowed amount is history; the control sheet needs today’s obligation and decision terms.

Choose one extra-payment method and record the reason. Highest-rate-first usually minimises interest; smallest-balance-first can simplify the queue; priority debt may require different treatment. The workbook should implement a conscious rule, not switch strategy whenever one balance feels uncomfortable.

Model scheduled minimums and planned extra principal separately. When one balance closes, roll the released payment to the next target automatically. A payoff date is an estimate dependent on rate, payment timing and no new borrowing, so label assumptions and compare them with actual statements.

Flag rate changes, promotional expiries and missed or returned payments. Alerts need lead time for action, not merely a red cell after the cost rises. Calendar a review before expiry and preserve the offer terms that created the deadline.

Do not use the workbook as a substitute for contacting a lender or qualified debt adviser when payments are at risk. In the United States, [[S1|Consumer Financial Protection Bureau tools]] explain debt and cash-flow resources; UK readers can use [[S2|MoneyHelper debt guidance]]. Local rights and priority debts differ.

When a debt is settled, retain the final statement or confirmation under an appropriate record policy, mark the account closed and remove it from current alerts. Do not delete prior payments from trend data or count the released minimum as new income.

sections.heading: Keep Investments in a Policy Lane
paragraphs: The control sheet should summarise investments without becoming a trading terminal. Record account, owner, wrapper or tax status, contribution, broad allocation, fees and current value. Security-level detail belongs only when it supports diversification, tax records or a defined rebalancing decision.

Separate contributions, withdrawals, income and market movement. A positive return is not saving, and a transfer between investment accounts is not a new contribution. Reconcile provider statements before calculating performance. Time-weighted or money-weighted returns answer different questions and should not be mixed casually.

Write target allocation ranges and a rebalancing rule. The dashboard should alert when allocation leaves the range or a planned review arrives, not whenever markets move. Frequent reaction increases cost, tax complexity and behavioural error without improving the policy.

Show concentration by employer, issuer, sector or geography where material. Several funds can hold the same largest companies. Include workplace shares and pensions in the household view. The [[S3|SEC Investor.gov diversification guide]] provides a starting point for understanding concentration and risk.

Record fees as amounts and rates when possible. Platform, fund, advice, trading and foreign-exchange costs can sit in different statements. Compare them with service received and account size. Do not treat the lowest fee as automatically best when the product, protection or access differs.

Protect near-term goals from market exposure. Link each investment account to its horizon and purpose. If money is needed soon, the dashboard should not celebrate a high expected return while ignoring the possibility of selling after a decline.

sections.heading: Add Tax and Records Without Building a Shadow Tax Office
paragraphs: Create a tax index rather than attempting to calculate every jurisdiction’s liability inside the workbook. List filing status, relevant accounts, income sources, expected forms, deadlines, estimated payments and evidence location. Use official current rules or qualified help for the return itself.

Track taxable interest, dividends, disposals, self-employment income and deductible or allowable expenses only where applicable. Preserve original provider statements and acquisition records. The U.S. [[S4|IRS recordkeeping guidance]] and [[S5|GOV.UK record guidance]] describe different obligations; use the authority for the relevant jurisdiction.

Reconcile payroll withholding or deductions with payslips and annual records. A projected refund is not income until filed and paid. A likely balance due belongs in a sinking fund before the deadline. Keep forecast, filed amount and settled amount in separate fields.

Do not upload identity documents, returns or full account identifiers to a shared workbook. Use restricted storage, retention limits and access logs where available. The sheet can point to an evidence code without containing the evidence itself.

Calendar filing, estimated payments, wrapper deadlines and document arrival. Lead indicators reduce last-minute errors. Set an owner and completion evidence for each task; a checkbox without a filed receipt or payment confirmation may provide false closure.

Archive each tax year after reconciliation and note unresolved items. Formula changes in the current workbook should not alter filed-year evidence. When the facts include multiple countries, businesses, equity compensation or trusts, seek qualified advice rather than expanding an amateur formula indefinitely.

sections.heading: Map Insurance, Dependants and Continuity
paragraphs: Create a protection register with policy type, insured person or asset, provider, coverage, excess or deductible, premium, renewal, beneficiaries where relevant and evidence location. The dashboard should reveal gaps and duplication without storing sensitive medical or identity details.

Link protection to the risk it covers: income interruption, death, disability, health costs, home, vehicle, liability or business disruption. A policy count does not measure resilience. Compare coverage with debts, dependants, employer benefits, emergency cash and actual replacement needs.

Record renewal and review dates early enough to compare. Premium alone is not the product; exclusions, waiting periods, limits, definitions and claim service matter. Verify changes in the issued documents rather than a phone summary.

Add dependants and essential responsibilities to a continuity page: regular support, care arrangements, key contacts and where authorised documents are held. Do not expose children’s or relatives’ private data broadly. The page should guide a trusted person to secure records, not duplicate them.

Document who can operate the money system during illness or incapacity, using lawful authority and secure access. Never place passwords in the workbook. Use password-manager emergency access or institution procedures appropriate to the household and jurisdiction.

Run an annual continuity test. Can the authorised person identify bills, income, insurance, debts and professional contacts without relying on one person’s memory? Record missing instructions and fix them. A sophisticated dashboard that only its creator can operate is a single point of failure.

sections.heading: Design the Dashboard Around Exceptions
paragraphs: The late photograph shows charts, a calculator, folders and people reviewing figures. It communicates the dashboard’s job: condense evidence into attention. Display no more than the measures required for the next decision—cash runway, due obligations, net-worth bridge, debt queue, goal status and unresolved items.

Use status colours sparingly and never rely on colour alone. Add words or icons such as on track, watch, action and incomplete. The site’s article graphics avoid green, and a workbook can also use accessible neutral, amber, red and blue states with text labels.

Every metric needs a definition, period, source and threshold. “Savings rate” is meaningless until the numerator and denominator are stated. “Emergency months” requires essential monthly spending and accessible designated cash. Place the definition close to the chart or in the dictionary.

Prioritise exceptions: unreconciled balance, missed income, bill due before cash, expired rate, reserve below floor, debt increase, goal contribution missed or insurance renewal approaching. A dashboard that reports only positive totals can hide operational failures.

Keep charts tied to action. A twelve-month spending line might trigger review after three months above threshold; a net-worth bridge might prompt investigation of a liability jump. Remove visualisations that never change a decision, even when they look impressive.

Test the dashboard on a small screen and in print or PDF if the household uses those formats. Freeze clear labels, avoid tiny charts and ensure totals remain understandable without hover effects. Accessibility and portability matter during an emergency or device change.

sections.heading: Secure the File Without Making It Unusable
paragraphs: Minimise data first. A control sheet usually needs account codes and balances, not full numbers, credentials, government identifiers or card details. Less sensitive data reduces harm from accidental sharing while preserving the decision function.

Use strong unique authentication and multi-factor authentication on the storage account. The U.S. [[S6|CISA MFA guidance]] explains why a second factor improves account protection. Review shared links, connected apps, former household members and recovery methods regularly.

Apply least privilege. A partner responsible for review may need edit access; an adviser may need a time-limited redacted export; a family contact may need emergency instructions rather than the live workbook. Public-link sharing is inappropriate for a financial dashboard.

Maintain version history and an independent backup. Test recovery by restoring a copy and checking formulas, links and evidence references. Synchronisation is not the same as backup: accidental deletion or corruption can sync to every device.

Protect imports and formulas. Treat downloaded files as untrusted, inspect columns and avoid enabling unknown macros or scripts. Document any automation, its permissions, error alerts and shutdown method. Convenience should not grant a budgeting add-on access to unrelated email or storage.

Create an exit plan for the tool. Export the workbook and dictionary to usable formats, document formulas and know what happens when a subscription ends. A personal control system should remain portable enough to survive a provider change.

sections.heading: Close the Month With a Fixed Sequence
paragraphs: Begin the monthly close after statements and major income have posted. Update the account register, import transactions, match transfers and reconcile each account. Do not review trends until the ledger difference is zero or a documented timing item explains it.

Next update balances, debt terms, goal funding and investment contributions. Build the net-worth bridge and accessible-cash figure. Confirm sinking funds still sum to their holding accounts. Resolve any case where one balance appears committed twice.

Then compare cash-flow plan with actual and inspect only material variances. Review the exception queue, upcoming due dates, promotional expiries, renewals and tax tasks. Turn each required response into an owner, action and deadline.

Finish by projecting the next pay cycle and executing approved transfers. Do not change long-term investment or debt policy because of one noisy month unless the underlying capacity or goal changed. Operational corrections and policy decisions belong to different review levels.

Save the close date, evidence period and version. Archive or lock the period, back up the file and remove temporary exports from downloads or shared folders when no longer needed. Temporary financial files are often the least protected copies.

Hold a short household review focused on decisions, not blame. Explain the largest movement, confirm next actions and note any change in work, care, health or goals. A control sheet succeeds when it supports a better conversation and timely action, not when every line is perfectly categorised.

Once a quarter, question the system itself. Are categories still useful? Do account totals reconcile quickly? Which alerts produced action, and which created noise? Remove fields that no longer support decisions and document any formula change before applying it to historical periods.

Review rates, fees, recurring commitments, insurance, asset allocation and debt order using current documents. Do not switch products merely because a comparison changed slightly. Include tax, access, protection, service and switching friction in the decision.

Stress one scenario: income pause, major repair, medical cost, relocation or market decline. Use the dashboard to identify cash runway, obligations that continue, optional transfers to pause and people to contact. The test should create a concrete improvement, not a dramatic forecast.

Audit access and recovery. Remove stale collaborators, test backup restoration and confirm the emergency operator can locate instructions. Update devices, recovery contacts and evidence references without placing secrets in the file.

Compare time spent with decisions improved. If monthly close takes hours and changes nothing, simplify imports, categories or charts. If important renewals or debts still surprise the household, strengthen the exception queue. Efficiency means reliable control with bounded maintenance.

Publish no personal dashboard screenshots. If sharing a lesson, rebuild it with fictional data and remove hidden metadata, comments and links. Redaction can miss formulas or revision history. Privacy is part of financial control, not an obstacle after the design is complete.

A mature control sheet should feel less exciting over time. Accounts reconcile, bills arrive as expected, reserves have owners and alerts are rare. Resist adding tabs to recreate novelty. Complexity earns its place only when a recurring decision cannot be made accurately without it.

Update after major life changes: job, partnership, child, move, property, business, inheritance or retirement. Revisit household boundaries, goals, insurance, access and tax records. Preserve the old version so scope changes do not overwrite the story of earlier periods.

Use official guidance for rules and providers for account facts. The workbook organises decisions; it does not determine legal rights, tax liability, insurance coverage or investment suitability. Record when qualified advice was used and the assumptions it addressed.

Keep one improvement backlog instead of editing formulas during every close. Prioritise errors, security and missing decisions before design. Test changes on a copy, reconcile outputs and document the release. A financial system deserves basic change control because silent errors can persist for years.

Measure success through faster reconciliation, fewer surprises, funded obligations and decisions completed on time. A beautiful chart that does not improve those outcomes is optional. A plain balance check that catches a missing payment is essential.

The control sheet is a household operating tool: a map of accounts, a reconciled cash ledger, an explanation of net worth, contracts for goals, queues for debt and action, and a secure review rhythm. Build the smallest version that produces trust, then maintain it long enough to become useful.

summary: A personal finance control sheet should answer what cash is available, what is due, why net worth changed, which goal is off course and what action has an owner. It is a decision surface, not a warehouse for every transaction and document.

Define fields, units, signs, dates, account codes, household boundaries, currencies and categories before entering data. Separate observed balances from plans and estimates. Validation can prevent typing errors, but statements and reconciliations remain the evidence.

Build an account register containing purpose, ownership, access, currency, balance date, rate, due date and status without storing passwords or full account numbers. Show accessible and restricted assets separately, and retain closed-account history outside current alerts.

Import transactions from statements, preserve raw descriptions, match transfers and reconcile opening balance plus activity to closing balance. Use a review queue for unresolved items and archive closed periods so corrections remain dated and explainable.

Model cash flow around payment timing, annual sinking funds and the lowest projected operating balance. Separate committed, expected and optional spending. Forecast uncertain income cautiously and convert material variance into a named action and deadline.

Use a net-worth bridge to separate contributions, debt principal, withdrawals and market movement. Show total and accessible net worth, keep interest separate from principal and document conservative valuation methods for illiquid assets.

Give goals an owner, target range, date, designated balance, contribution and priority. Ensure one savings balance is not promised to several goals. Record planned withdrawals as successful use and archive inactive goals.

Operate debt through a verified register and payoff queue. Track rates, minimums, dates and promotional expiry, separate planned extra principal and roll released payments forward. Seek official or qualified help early when required payments are at risk.

Summarise investments by purpose, contribution, allocation, fees and value rather than turning the sheet into a trading screen. Separate contributions from returns, define rebalancing ranges, expose concentration and keep near-term goals outside inappropriate market risk.

Use a tax index for deadlines, forms, payments and evidence location, relying on current official rules for actual filing. Keep sensitive returns and identifiers outside broadly shared workbooks, and archive filed periods from later formula changes.

Map insurance, dependants and continuity. Link each policy to a risk, record renewal and coverage, and document how an authorised person can operate essential finances without placing credentials in the workbook.

Design the dashboard around exceptions such as unreconciled balances, low cash, missed contributions, expiring rates and approaching renewals. Define every metric and threshold, use text with colour and remove charts that never lead to decisions.

Secure the system through data minimisation, strong authentication, least-privilege sharing, version history, tested backups and careful imports. Maintain portable exports and a documented exit route from the software provider.

Close monthly in a fixed order: register, import, transfer match, reconciliation, balances, net-worth bridge, variance, exceptions, actions and next-pay-cycle transfers. Review the system quarterly, stress one disruption and simplify any work that does not improve control.

A mature sheet becomes boring and dependable. Measure it by faster reconciliation, fewer surprises, funded obligations and timely decisions. Add complexity only when a recurring decision genuinely requires it, and preserve change history when formulas or household scope change.

Keep source evidence separate from the control file. The workbook may reference a statement, contract, tax record or invoice without embedding sensitive documents in a broadly shared surface. Use account codes instead of full identifiers, restrict collaborators, review shared links and remove temporary exports after legitimate use. Portability also matters: document formulas, keep usable exports and know how the household will leave the current software without losing its financial history or operating instructions. Preserve a dated recovery test.

faq.question: How many tabs should a personal finance workbook have?
faq.answer: Use only the registers, ledgers and views needed for recurring decisions. The correct number is the smallest structure that reconciles reliably and explains actions.

faq.question: Should every transaction be categorised?
faq.answer: Every material transaction should reconcile, but category detail should serve a decision. Use a review queue for unresolved items rather than expanding categories endlessly.

faq.question: Should passwords or account numbers be stored in the sheet?
faq.answer: No. Use account codes, restricted evidence storage and a reputable password manager or institution process. Minimise sensitive data and avoid public links.

faq.question: How often should net worth be updated?
faq.answer: Monthly is sufficient for many households, with deeper quarterly reconciliation. Illiquid assets should follow a documented evidence-based valuation frequency rather than guessed monthly changes.

faq.question: How should couples share the workbook?
faq.answer: Define ownership for each close, grant least-privilege access and hold a short decision review. Both adults should understand essential accounts and continuity instructions.

faq.question: What makes a dashboard trustworthy?
faq.answer: Each figure has a definition, period, source and formula; account balances reconcile; forecasts are labelled; and unresolved differences remain visible until closed.

faq.question: How should the workbook be backed up?
faq.answer: Use version history plus an independent backup, test restoration and preserve portable exports and documentation. Synchronisation alone does not protect against every deletion or corruption.

glossary.definition: A decision-focused workbook that summarises reconciled financial records, status and actions.
Definitions for fields, units, signs, dates, allowed values and sources.
The inventory of financial accounts, ownership, purpose, access and operating details.
Proof that opening balance plus period activity equals the verified closing balance.
A temporary holding place for unresolved entries that must be investigated.
An explanation of change through contributions, withdrawals, debt principal and valuation movement.
Cash accumulated progressively for a known future expense.
Prioritised unresolved items with an owner, action and deadline.
Granting only the access required for a person’s legitimate role.
The fixed process that reconciles records and finalises a financial period.
